text: Do you know why the tallest building on Earth is shaped like a desert flower?
This is Burj Khalifa, in Dubai. Eight hundred and twenty-eight metres tall. A hundred and sixty-three floors.
Up there, its biggest enemy isn't its own weight. It's the wind.
When wind flows past a tall tower, it peels off in swirls. First on one side, then the other. Like a flag flapping in the breeze.
Every swirl gives the tower a little push. If the pushes keep the same rhythm, the tower starts to rock. And the rocking grows.
So the architects borrowed the shape of a desert flower. Three wings, in a Y.
And as the tower rises, the wings step back, twenty-seven times, in a spiral.
Every few floors, the wind meets a different shape. The swirls never line up, and never find a rhythm. Engineers call it confusing the wind.
The very top still moves. About one and a half metres. Slowly, like a tree.
Inside, a six-sided concrete core runs up the middle. And the three wings brace it from every side, like the legs of a tripod.
The concrete was pumped six hundred and six metres straight up. A world record.
Underneath, it stands on a hundred and ninety-two concrete piles. Each one and a half metres wide, buried more than fifty metres deep in the desert.
And on top, a spire of more than four thousand tonnes of steel, so tall it could be a skyscraper on its own.
No single weak point. That's how Orbi Transfer sends your biggest files.
A big file is split into parts, and several travel at once.
Lose the signal, and it picks up right where it left off. No app, no login.
